title: One Thousand and One Nights (Scheherazade)
subtitle: Telling stories to survive
subject: mythologie
description: Scheherazade survives 1,001 nights by telling stories. A collection born between Persia, Baghdad and Egypt, now a myth the whole world knows.

hero.hook: Every night, a woman tells a story so that she will still be alive at dawn.

blocks.text: The **One Thousand and One Nights** (*Alf Layla wa-Layla*) is not the work of a single author. It is a palimpsest: centuries of tales, spoken and written, Indian, Persian, Arab and Egyptian.

At the center sits a dizzying idea: a woman, **Scheherazade**, turns storytelling into a shield. As long as she keeps talking, the king who wanted her dead has to wait. Here is how speech becomes a weapon of survival.

sections.title: An architecture of paper: how a world-text was born

blocks.text: The core comes from a Persian stock of tales, the [[Hazār Afsāna]] (“A Thousand Tales”), themselves fed by Indian tradition. In Baghdad, under the [[Abbasids]] (8th to 13th centuries), the collection turned Arabic: urban legends, court anecdotes, a tone that could turn satirical.

blocks.caption: A manuscript of the Nights: a world-text still taking shape

blocks.text: “A thousand and one” is not an exact count. In Arabic the figure suggests abundance, almost infinity. Some scribes even read it as a charm against the evil eye.

In Egypt, in the time of the [[Mamluks]], new cycles were added. A surprise for Western readers: **Aladdin** and **Ali Baba** are missing from the medieval Arabic manuscripts. They are “orphan tales,” which entered the book later, by way of Europe.

sections.title: The power of Scheherazade: storytelling as a shield

blocks.text: King **Shahryar**, betrayed by his first wife, marries a young woman every evening and has her killed at dawn. **Scheherazade**, the vizier's daughter, offers herself. She begins a story, then stops at the tensest moment.

blocks.caption: Scheherazade facing Shahryar: storytelling as a shield

blocks.text: She piles up [[nested stories (frame narrative)]]: a character tells a tale in which another character tells a third. The king, caught by the need to hear the rest, puts off the execution. After **a thousand and one nights**, listening has changed Shahryar: he can feel for other people again. Scheherazade did not only entertain him. She repaired a tyrant.

sections.title: The turn to Europe and the making of a myth

blocks.text: Between **1704** and **1717**, the French orientalist **Antoine Galland** published his translation. He shaped the text to the taste of the court of **Louis XIV** and added tales he had heard from [[Hanna Diyab]], a Syrian visitor passing through Paris. That is how Aladdin joined the collection.

blocks.caption: Galland opens the Nights to 18th century Europe

blocks.text: Young men sometimes woke Galland at night by shouting under his window: “Monsieur Galland, if you are not asleep, tell us one of your stories!”

Its success invented a [[European orientalism]]: flying carpets, genies, caliphs in disguise. The vision was a fantasy, often a crude one, but its influence was enormous, from **Proust** to **Borges**, who saw in these narrative loops the very image of literary infinity.

sections.title: A modern book and its philosophy

blocks.text: Why tell stories? The Nights answer: to hold death at a distance. As long as Scheherazade's voice can be heard, the fatal dawn is put off. Fiction gives shape to chaos.
That machinery still drives our television series: the [[cliffhanger]], the cut made right at the edge of the drop, comes straight from her. A book open onto infinity, refusing to close.
**Scheherazade** survives **1,001** nights by nesting story inside story: she invents suspense as a survival tool and turns speech into political power.
